title: Monash Uni to offer AI cybersecurity degree
full_text:
A shortage of cybersecurity experts has left Australian organisations vulnerable as state-backed hackers and criminal gangs harness artificial intelligence to accelerate their attacks, warns the head of one of the country's most prominent cybersecurity firms.
CyberCX founder and chief executive John Paitaridis believes there is a simple solution: "We've got to prepare the next generation of cybersecurity professionals to be more AI literate. That's the strategic imperative; we need to tackle this head-on."
CyberCX has teamed up with Monash University to co-design and help teach a new specialised Bachelor of CyberAI degree.
The qualification, which links AI and cybersecurity over a three-year program, will be launched on Wednesday, with the first cohort of students expected to start the first semester next year.
Monash University vice chancellor Sharon Pickering said: "We know that sovereign capability around AI and sovereign capability around AI cybersecurity is critical. We need to keep up.
"Right now, there is a clear need for Australia to have a specialised AI cybersecurity workforce, and we are leaning into that challenge."
Research by Accenture, which acquired CyberCX last year, found that nearly 50 per cent of all cybersecurity roles globally remained open and unfilled.
The federal government's 2023-30 cybersecurity strategy notes that employers face a shortage of skilled cyber professionals and "a mismatch between job requirements and employee skills". "A lack of sufficient job-ready experience is a key challenge for industry, with graduates and workforce entrants often requiring further on-the-job training to become proficient," the strategy, released in 2023, showed.
Paitaridis said the widespread availability of AI had made it easier for nefarious actors, and he believed AI should be taught as a key component of every university course.
"We're adopting this explosion of these AI models, but we don't have the cybersecurity workforce that's capable of defending and protecting our organisations and institutions," he said.
"We wouldn't look at a cybersecurity professional now without having a foundation of understanding of the AI capability, AI risks and the ability to be able to defend against these."
Universities across the board are scrambling to find ways to embed the rapidly changing technology in existing coursework, responding to calls from industries that increasingly view AI fluency as a baseline expectation of graduates.
In a parliamentary submission last month, the Future Skills Organisation warned that employers in the finance, business and tech sectors were having to pick up the cost of training graduates who arrived in the workforce bereft of digital and AI skills.
The new dean of business and economics at Melbourne University, Professor Serge da Motta Veiga, is starting the process of integrating AI into the faculty's programs.
"The goal for me is equipping our students with skills where they will challenge AI, so that they can learn when AI can be helpful and when AI can actually hinder their critical thinking," he said. "This is what companies want from their workforce.
"Quite a few of our courses are doing that, but it's not uniform. And we're also not starting early enough."
Da Motta Veiga, who was most recently at France's NEOMA Business School, said Australian universities were "falling a bit behind" in their approach to research compared with competitors in China, Hong Kong and Singapore, which he said were less risk-averse.
"We are innovative here in Australia, but I think we can be more innovative ... we cannot be afraid of making mistakes," he said. "We need to take more risks, get a little bit out of our comfort zone, and try new things."
